source.title: Meta Models: Models that Model Learning

page_placements.theme: Extrapolation depends on functional form, fitting and identification

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates held-out loss prediction and extrapolation, including parametric scaling-law baselines, with a different method and benchmark setup from the original scaling-law studies.
record.gate_note: The rows below cover reported held-out prediction errors for parametric scaling-law baselines, the Delphi scaling ladder, the Marin Hero Run forecast, and downstream-accuracy prediction. Other reported TabPFN comparisons, hyperparameter selection results, and internal-observable predictions do not themselves test the claim versions listed.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates a frozen TabPFN meta-model for predicting training outcomes. Scaling laws enter only as tools and comparators: Chinchilla-law residual offsets, parametric-law baselines, and the Marin official law as a reference for the Hero Run. The study never asks whether loss follows a power law, whether fits on small runs extrapolate as a general property, or whether downstream accuracy scales predictably. The baseline-law MAEs are reported only to rank predictors, with no reference scale for judging the laws themselves. The downstream rows (R19–R21) measure TabPFN's own prediction error, not how downstream accuracy behaves with scale. A case for T5 on V2 could rest on the Delphi Chinchilla extrapolation error (0.149 nats at up to 333× compute). That number is one baseline fit compared against learned predictors, with no analysis of the law, so it is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that a frozen off-the-shelf TabPFN, treating training records as numeric data, matches or beats a fine-tuned LLM meta-model (NCPL) across final-loss, curve, downstream, observable and selection tasks at far lower cost. They report that KAN-learned coordinates further help on StepLaw and that conditioning on a run prefix improved the Hero Run forecast. They state that reliable extrapolation beyond observed conditions remains a challenge and that lower prediction error alone does not establish compute savings.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates a numerical in-context predictor and parametric-law baselines on heterogeneous training-record corpora; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law fitting protocol.
record.method_sensitivity: Results depend on corpus, ID versus OOD split, available configuration and recipe fields, context records, and target processing. The Hero forecast with a target-run prefix uses different information from the official law. The paper also reports that removing DataDecide recipe identity increases OOD final-loss MAE from 0.0178 to 0.1117.

fits_no_version.finding: A Chinchilla law fitted on Delphi runs of 3e18–3e20 FLOPs has MAE 0.149 nats on held-out runs at 1e21–1e23 FLOPs. The Delphi team's own forecast (cited) has 0.0182 and residual TabPFN has 0.0093.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A simple Chinchilla-form fit can extrapolate final loss poorly over 100× compute, while other fitting approaches extrapolate well. This bears on fit-dependence if tested directly.

fits_no_version.finding: Parametric L=E+A/N^α+B/D^β baselines have higher held-out MAE than TabPFN, XGBoost and NCPL on Marin, StepLaw, MoE and DataDecide. Their curve MAEs are very large, e.g. 0.80 on Marin ID.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Configuration-agnostic parametric loss laws are less accurate predictors of individual-run loss than learned predictors that use optimizer and recipe fields.

fits_no_version.finding: The Marin official law (L=1.5+AC^-α per progress value) has MAE 0.0576 on 14 early Hero Run checkpoints, versus 0.0216 for TabPFN using the target-run prefix.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ladder-based scaling-law forecasts of a much larger MoE run's early loss trajectory carry errors of about 0.06 nats.

record.problems: The paper states that reliable extrapolation beyond observed training conditions remains a challenge. The Hero Run score covers only 14 subsequent checkpoints through 14.61% of training; its completion forecast remains untested, and the official law and TabPFN forecast use different information. DataDecide evaluations end before planned training completion for some sizes, and the 1B downstream predictions remain biased low. Many main-table numbers are point estimates without uncertainty intervals.
record.rows_left_out: No additional directly relevant parametric-law or scaling-ladder results were identified beyond the listed final-loss/curve metrics and the Delphi and Hero Run forecasts. Other predictor results, such as TabPFN comparisons, are not results of the power-law claim itself.

untested.parts: All: no test of power-law form of loss in N, D or C.
No systematic test of whether small-run power-law fits predict much larger runs. Law errors appear only as predictor baselines.
All: no other modalities or training regimes.
No measurement of downstream accuracy versus scale or loss. Only TabPFN prediction error is reported.
No analysis of how exponents or allocations depend on fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's labels are removed because the study is T4. Several Table 1 rows have wrong values: R4 and R8 report RMSE as MAE; R9–R12 report sparsity-aware-law values under the parametric-law label. R17's per-budget numbers are TabPFN's. If curators prefer treating the Delphi Chinchilla baseline as a V2/V7 test, it would at most be limits_scope from one fit, against a cited stronger forecast.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports prediction errors for parametric loss-law baselines, but does not directly measure whether held-out pretraining loss follows a power law over several orders of magnitude while the other quantities are non-bottlenecks.
The study does not establish a general extrapolation guarantee across model families or training setups.
It does not test the compute-optimal parameter-count/token-count allocation or estimate how those quantities grow with compute.
It does not compare depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
It evaluates language-model training records and downstream scores, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds in other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.

The reported downstream evaluation is on DataDecide OLMo runs and ten OLMES tasks; it does not test predictability across arbitrary downstream tasks or establish a relation specifically to pretraining loss.
Although the paper discusses setup-dependent prediction and limitations of extrapolation, it does not test how power-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations change with fitting choices.
